sections.title: The Benefits of Glide Path Analysis

body.text: A glide path is built around assumptions about how participants save, retire, and use their assets. We compare those assumptions with your actual workforce demographics to determine whether the strategy reasonably fits your plan.

Your committee should be able to explain why the selected TDF’s glide path is appropriate. We document the factors reviewed, alternatives considered, and rationale behind the decision so your fiduciary file reflects a clear, prudent process.

Same-vintage funds can hold materially different levels of equity exposure. Glide path analysis helps your committee understand how much risk participants are taking at different stages and whether that risk profile aligns with retirement behavior.

Fund manufacturers naturally explain why their approach is the right one. As an independent, fee-only advisor, PointOak evaluates glide paths without a product incentive, giving your committee a more neutral basis for comparison.

A glide path that is too aggressive or too conservative for your workforce can affect retirement outcomes. We evaluate both growth potential and downside exposure in the context of your participants’ time horizons and expected withdrawal patterns.

sections.title: What We Evaluate in a TDF Glide Path

body.text: We review how much of the portfolio remains invested in equities throughout the glide path, particularly as participants approach and move into retirement.
We look beyond the stock percentage to understand how the fund uses bonds, cash, and other asset classes as risk declines.
We evaluate when the fund reaches its most conservative allocation and whether that philosophy fits participant withdrawal behavior.
The glide path should make sense for the workforce using it.
Glide paths can change over time as providers update assumptions and investment strategies. We evaluate whether the current structure still fits your plan.

sections.title: Who Benefits Most from Glide Path Analysis?

body.text: If the plan simply adopted a recordkeeper's standard target date series, the glide path may never have been independently evaluated against your participant population.
Changes in employee age, turnover, compensation, or retirement behavior can alter whether the assumptions behind your existing TDF remain appropriate.
A provider transition often means evaluating a different TDF lineup. It's an ideal time to compare glide paths independently before selecting the new default.

items.title: Your Committee Can't Explain the Current Strategy

body.text: If committee members know which target date fund is used but can't explain why its glide path fits participants, a documented analysis can strengthen the decision-making process.
When competing funds have similar fees and performance, glide path differences often become one of the most important distinctions between them.

items.title: When Another Glide Path Review May Not Be Necessary

body.text: If your plan completed a documented, independent TDF review recently and there have been no meaningful changes to the fund strategy, workforce demographics, or plan objectives, your existing monitoring process may be sufficient.

items.q: What is a target date fund glide path?

a.text: A glide path is the schedule a target date fund follows as it gradually shifts from growth-oriented investments toward a more conservative asset allocation.
It determines how much equity, fixed income, and other asset classes the fund holds at different points before and after the target retirement date.

items.q: What's the difference between a “to” and “through” glide path?

a.text: A “to” glide path generally reaches its most conservative allocation around retirement, while a “through” glide path continues reducing risk after retirement.
The right choice depends on how participants are expected to use their assets once they retire.

items.q: Are all target date funds with the same retirement year similar?

a.text: Two funds labeled 2040 can have materially different equity exposure, fixed-income allocations, diversification, fees, and post-retirement strategies.

items.q: How much equity should a TDF hold at retirement?

a.text: There is no single appropriate percentage for every plan.
The right level depends on participant behavior, expected retirement timing, withdrawal patterns, longevity considerations, and the overall philosophy of the target date strategy.

items.q: How often should a glide path be reviewed?

a.text: Glide path suitability should be reviewed periodically as part of the plan's ongoing TDF monitoring process.
A new review may also be warranted when participant demographics change, the provider modifies its strategy, or the plan changes recordkeepers.

items.q: Can a target date fund be too conservative?

a.text: It can be too conservative for a particular participant population, just as another fund may be too aggressive.
The issue isn't whether the glide path is inherently conservative or aggressive. It's whether the risk profile reasonably aligns with the needs and behavior of the plan's participants.

items.q: Why does participant behavior matter when evaluating a glide path?

a.text: A participant who withdraws assets immediately at retirement has different risk considerations than someone who leaves the account invested for another 20 years.
Understanding how participants typically use the plan helps your committee evaluate whether a “to” or “through” strategy—and the level of equity exposure around retirement—makes sense.
